Mechanical assembly · Revision 4.1

NFC Player
Case

Charcoal printed case with a brass face set inside a thin printed rim, a card that leans back in a slot, and a tray in the lid for five spare cards.

200 × 128 × 59 mm printed shell. Knob, screw heads, feet and cards stand proud of it; the key caps sit flush with the brass.

What goes where

The numbers on each picture are explained in the list under it. Hover a number or a line to pick out the other. The bought parts are simple blocks at their nominal size and position: they show where things go and which way round, not exactly what they look like.

Changes in revision 4.1

Measure first

Published drawings did not settle these, so each is a named value at the top of case.py with a sensible default. Measure your parts, change the value and rebuild before printing the front or rear panel or cutting brass.

AreaChangeWhy
KeysThe Kailh Choc switches and their keycaps are gone. Each key is now a printed cap, 14 mm square, that slides in a hole through the brass and the panel with its face flush with the brass, and presses a 6 × 6 mm tactile switch soldered to the front board. See Keys, knob and power key.Keyboard switches need 3 mm of travel in front of the panel, so their caps stood about 7.5 mm proud with a gap behind them. The tactile switches click after about 0.25 mm, like a hi-fi button.
SpacerA new printed part, board-spacer.stl, 2.5 mm thick, between the panel and the front board. It has an opening round each key for the cap's lip and the switch, and openings for the board's solder joints.It sets the switches just behind the caps. The panel itself stays 4.2 mm thick, so nothing else moves.
Front boardRevision 2: the four hot-swap sockets are replaced by the tactile switches, on the side facing the panel. Its top edge is 51.5 mm up (was 53) to clear the card tray now that it sits further back. The board's screws are M2 × 6 (were M2 × 4).The switches are soldered straight on, with no sockets.
Front panel and brassA 14.4 mm square hole for each key in the panel, and 14.6 mm in the brass, with rounded corners. The pockets for the switch clips and the board's solder joints are gone from the panel.The holes guide the caps; the solder joints now sit in the spacer.
ValueDefaultWhat to measure
LCD_OFF_X, LCD_OFF_Z2, 0Where the lit area's centre sits relative to the centre of the 58 × 35 mm screen board, seen from the front. Set from Waveshare's outline drawing of the 2inch LCD Module: the picture sits about 2 mm right of centre with the pin pads on the left. Fit the board that way round, or change the sign. The bracket's screw slots let the screen move 2 mm either way sideways; to move it further, or up or down, change these and reprint the bracket.

Check the holes pass your plugs' metal shells, not just the sockets' barrels. See the board stack drawing for the heights assumed.

Print the fit gauge first and try your encoder in it: its thread must pass 2.3 mm of panel and brass and still take the washer and nut.

Print

Millimetres, 100% scale. Start with a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.20 mm layers, four walls and 20% infill in PETG. The largest part is 200 mm long and fits a 220 × 220 mm bed.

FileOrientation and notes
fit-gauge.stlFlat, pocket up. Print it first. It has a key cap's square hole, the encoder hole and its pocket, 3.3, 2.55 and 2.9 mm holes, the 55.4 × 1.65 mm card slot and a corner of the brass pocket.
chassis.stlFloor down, no support. Clear the horizontal screw pilots in the towers by hand.
lid.stlTop surface down, with support under the two curved edges.
front.stlInside face down, brass pocket up, no support.
board-spacer.stlFlat, either face down.
keycap-previous.stl, keycap-play.stl, keycap-next.stl, keycap-back.stlFace down, no support: the face comes out as smooth as the bed. 0.12 mm layers make the symbols sharper. Try one in the fit gauge's square hole: it should slide freely without rattling. Fill the symbols with paint if you like.
rear.stlFlat, either face down.
card-guide.stlFoot down, brim if needed. Keep support out of the card channel.
display-cradle.stlBase down, as it stands in the case. No support.

Hardware

  • M3 screws that thread straight into the print (try one in the gauge first, and drive by hand): four M3 × 10 for the front (they pass the brass and panel), four M3 × 8 for the rear, four low-profile M3 × 6 for the lid (head at most 6 mm across and 1.5 mm tall), two M3 × 6 for the card guide and two for the screen bracket, each with a washer.
  • Four M2.5 × 5 screws to hold the screen's standoffs to its bracket (check the thread of the standoffs on your screen).
  • Four M2.5 standoffs 5 mm tall, four M2.5 × 6 screws from below, and four more on top for the Pi.
  • Three M2 × 6 pan-head screws for the front board, threaded through the spacer and into the panel.
  • A 40-way IDC ribbon cable for the Raspberry Pi, female at both ends with both plugs on the same side of the cable (the usual kind), as short as you can find: about 10 cm. The run is about 6 cm, and a longer cable just bows upward under the lid.
  • Keys, knob and power key: four tactile switches (they go on the board), an encoder, a knob and a lit push button, all bought; the key caps are printed. See Keys, knob and power key for exactly what to get, and Front board for the board and its parts.
  • A panel-mount USB-C socket on a short lead ending in micro-USB.
  • 0.8 mm brass sheet and thin double-sided tape. Four feet at least 5 mm tall. Foam pads, female-to-female jumper leads, and thin hook-up wire for the encoder and power key.

Keys, knob and power key

The keys are printed caps that press small tactile switches on the front board. The knob sits on a rotary encoder, and the power key is a panel push button with a light in it. Those are bought parts, held by the printed front panel, and the brass covers its face.

What to buy

PartGetMake sure
Key switches ×46 × 6 mm through-hole tactile switches, 5 mm tall with the button (often sold as "6x6x5 mm")Four legs on a 6.5 × 4.5 mm grid, and a body 3.5 mm tall. Measure one: if it is not 5 mm from its base to the top of the button, set TACT_H in case.py and rebuild, and the spacer changes to suit. Buy plenty; they come in packs.
EncoderEC11-style rotary encoder with push switch: the Pi Hut one from the build guide, a Bourns PEC11R or an Alps EC11An M7 threaded bushing at least 5 mm long, a 6 mm shaft that reaches at least 12 mm past the bushing, and a nut and washer (usually included). Try it in the fit gauge first.
KnobSolid metal knob, up to 30 mm across, for a 6 mm shaftFixed with a set screw, and its bore matches your shaft's shape (D-flat or knurled).
Power key12 mm panel push button with a lit ring or power symbol, black plastic or metalMomentary, not latching or self-locking. The 12.2 mm hole fits a 12 mm thread; its nut at most 16 mm across and the body at most 30 mm deep. An LED rated 3 V, or 5–6 V (those have a resistor inside: fit a wire link for R2 on the board). A 12 V or 24 V one will not light.
WireThin hook-up wire and female jumper leadsThe encoder and power key have solder tags, not connectors: solder a wire to each and finish it with a female jumper end for the board's pin headers.

How the keys feel

A short, firm press with a click after about 0.25 mm, like the buttons on hi-fi gear. The click comes from the switch: cheap packs differ, so if you want a crisper or lighter one, any 6 × 6 mm through-hole switch of the same height fits.

How they are held

  • Key caps: each slides in its 14.4 mm square hole, face flush with the brass. A lip round its back stops it at the inside of the panel, so it cannot fall out of the front. Its back is hollow, and the switch stands inside it, 0.1 mm short of the back of the face. The switch's button pushes the cap back out after a press. Nothing holds a cap but the panel and the board, so take the board off to change one.
  • Key switches: soldered to the front of the front board, the side facing the panel. A printed spacer between panel and board sets the gap, and the board's three screws hold the lot together.
  • Encoder: held by its own nut. It goes in from behind with the threaded bushing through the 7.3 mm hole. On the front, a washer and then the nut clamp the brass and the 1.5 mm of plastic between the nut and the encoder body. The body also sits in a rectangular pocket, so it cannot turn when you twist the knob.
  • Locating lug: many encoders have a small lug beside the bushing, meant for a hole in a metal panel. The pocket already stops the encoder turning, so nip the lug off flush with side cutters, or the body will not sit flat.
  • Knob: slides onto the shaft and is held by its set screw on the shaft's flat. Leave about 1 mm between the knob and the nut so it never rubs.
  • Power key: goes in from the front through the 12.2 mm hole; its nut tightens from behind. Its body reaches past the front left corner tower, which is cut away for it between 16 and 43 mm up.
The smooth Bourns EM14 encoder mentioned in the build guide as a later upgrade has a different bushing and body, and needs 5 V and two resistor dividers that the board does not have. Check its drawing against the encoder hole and pocket and change ENCODER_HOLE and ENCODER_BODY in case.py, and wire it as the build guide describes.

Front board

A small printed circuit board, 84 × 47.5 mm, lies flat on a 2.5 mm printed spacer behind the front panel, behind the four keys. The keys' tactile switches are soldered to its front. A 40-way ribbon joins its box header to the pins on top of the DAC, so it reaches every pin of the Pi. The screen, NFC reader, knob and power key each plug into a labelled pin header on it. It also carries the two diodes the power key needs, and a transistor that lights the power key from 5 V.

Order it

The board is drawn in KiCad by front-board/board.py from the numbers in case.py, so it always matches the panel. Upload front-board/fab/nfc-front-board-gerbers.zip to any board maker (JLCPCB, PCBWay, Aisler and others). Choose 2 layers, 1.6 mm FR-4, any colour and any finish. No assembly service is needed. Five boards usually cost a few pounds plus postage. The schematic is in front-board/fab/nfc-front-board-schematic.pdf, and the KiCad project in front-board/ opens in KiCad 10 if you want to change anything.

Build it

  1. Every part but the key switches goes on the back: the side with the part labels. The front is marked This side towards the panel.
  2. Then the low parts: D1 and D2 with their stripe on the band printed on the board, R1 (1 kΩ), R2 (220 Ω, or a wire link if the power key's LED has its own resistor), and Q1 with its flat side on the flat of its outline.
  3. Then the pin headers and the 40-pin box header, its notch where the board shows it. Hold each one square while you solder the first pin.
  4. On the front, trim every lead to 1.5 mm or less, so the joints fit in the spacer's openings.
  5. Last, the four key switches on the front, in the squares marked for them. Push each fully home so it sits flat and square; a tilted switch tilts its cap. Solder them from the back, and trim their legs too.
  6. With a multimeter, check there is no short between 3.3 V, 5 V and ground: pins 1, 2 and 6 of the box header.

What plugs in where

HeaderForPins, from pin 1Lead
J2 LCDScreen1 VCC · 2 GND · 3 DIN · 4 CLK · 5 CS · 6 DC · 7 RST · 8 BLThe lead that comes with the Waveshare screen: its plug into the screen, its eight female ends onto these pins, by name.
J3 NFCNFC reader1 SCK · 2 MISO · 3 MOSI · 4 SS · 5 VCC · 6 GNDSix female-to-female leads to the reader's pins of the same names. Leave its IRQ and RSTO pins free.
J5 PWRPower key1 KEY · 2 GND · 3 LED+ · 4 LED-Four wires soldered to the button. KEY and GND go to its switch tags (either way round); LED+ and LED− to its lamp tags, the right way round.
J6 OLEDOLED (instead of the screen)1 GND · 2 VCC · 3 SCL · 4 SDAOnly if you use the 0.91-inch OLED: four leads to the OLED's pins of the same names.
J4 ENCKnob (encoder)1 A · 2 C · 3 B · 4 SW · 5 SWFive wires soldered to the encoder, ending in female leads. A, C and B are its three-pin side, C in the middle; the two SW pins are the push switch.

The keys need no leads: their switches are on the board. The keys and the knob only pull a pin to ground, and the Pi's own pull-ups hold them high. The power key reaches GPIO 24 and GPIO 3 through D1 and D2, exactly as in the build guide. GPIO 22 still switches the light, through Q1, so nothing changes in the software or in config.txt.

The box header sits straight in front of the Pi's header, the same way round: pin 1 on the right seen from the front, on the lower row. So the ribbon leaves the board, bends once and comes down onto the DAC's pins, with no twist or fold. The ribbon's red stripe marks pin 1 at both ends. On the board, pin 1 is at the triangle beside the box header, and its notch only lets the plug in one way. On the DAC there is no notch, so check before you push it on: pin 1 is the corner pin with a square pad on the Pi, at the right-hand end seen from the front of the case, and with the Pi running it reads 3.3 V, while its neighbour across the header (pin 2) reads 5 V.

Assembly

Printed part fitted in this stepPrinted parts already in placeBrassArrow: direction of fitting

1Fit the brass

  1. Deburr the brass and try it in the pocket. It should drop in with a hair of clearance and sit flush with the rim.
  2. Stick it down with thin double-sided tape, lining the screw holes up with the panel's.

2Fit the power key, the key caps and the encoder

Solder four wires to the power key and five to the encoder first, each ending in a female jumper end (see What plugs in where). It is easier before they are in the panel. Then:

  1. Push the power key in from the front and tighten its nut from behind, with its tags pointing down or sideways.
  2. Lay the panel face down. Drop each key cap into its hole from behind, face first, until its lip stops it. From the front, left to right: previous, play/pause, next, back, so from behind they read back, next, play/pause, previous.
  3. Nip off the encoder's locating lug if it has one. From behind, put the bushing through its hole so the body drops into the rectangular pocket.
  4. On the front: washer, then nut. Tighten the nut firmly with a spanner, holding the body square in its pocket.
  5. Slide the knob on, leaving about 1 mm clear of the nut, and tighten its set screw onto the flat of the shaft.

3Fit the spacer and the front board

  1. Build the board first (see Front board).
  2. Press the ribbon's plug onto the board's box header now, red stripe at the triangle. It is hard to reach once the board is on.
  3. With the panel still face down and the caps in their holes, lay the spacer on the back of the panel, over the caps' lips, its screw holes over the panel's.
  4. Lay the board on the spacer, switches down towards the caps (see the close-up of one key).
  5. Fit its three M2 × 6 screws, snug only: they thread into the spacer and the panel.
  6. Turn it over and press each key: it should click, and spring back flush. A key that is already pressed in or rattles means a switch of a different height; see TACT_H.

4Fit the front panel and the screen

  1. Screw the front panel to the chassis with four M3 × 10 screws. The power key's body passes the front left corner tower through its notch.
  2. Leave the four brass standoffs on the screen board. Screw the board to the bracket from behind with four M2.5 screws through the standoffs, glass facing away from the bracket and the socket on its open side. Leave them a little loose.
  3. Stand the bracket behind the window, socket on the right by the knob, and put its two M3 × 6 screws and washers through the base's slots into the floor bosses, loosely.
  4. Push the bracket forward until the glass touches the panel, then tighten its two floor screws.
  5. Look through the window and slide the screen sideways in its slots until the lit area is centred, then tighten its four screws.
  6. Push the lead's plug into the socket from the right, then bend the wires back towards the rear, clear of the encoder. A foam pad between the bracket and the lid stops it rattling.

5Mount the Pi and the DAC

  1. Screw four standoffs up through the two floor slots and leave them loose.
  2. Screw the Pi onto them, header at the front. Plug the DAC straight onto the Pi, checking pin 1. The pins of its header stand up through it, ready for the ribbon.
  3. Slide the stack back until the DAC's rear edge is {n(c.DAC_GAP)} mm from the rear panel's place (hold the panel on to check the sockets line up with its holes), then tighten the standoffs from below.

6Fit the card guide and the NFC reader

  1. Screw the guide to the two floor bosses with M3 × 6 screws. The slot leans back toward the top.
  2. Set the reader's switches for SPI. Slide it down into the middle pair of grooves in the two posts, antenna side toward the card and header at the top. That holds it 20 mm behind the card, where it reads best; this reader misses cards held right against it.
  3. Try a card. If reads are unreliable, move the reader to the front or rear grooves (16 or 24 mm). The lid stops it lifting out, so no tie or glue is needed.

7Wire it

  1. Run the ribbon straight back from the board and bend it down onto the pins on top of the DAC, red stripe on pin 1. It needs no twist and no fold.
  2. Plug the leads into the board's headers as the table under What plugs in where says: screen to LCD, reader to NFC, knob to ENC, power key to PWR.
  3. Keep the ribbon and leads out from under the card tray, which comes down to 52 mm over the left two thirds of the case, and clear of the card slot. Leave enough slack that the front panel can come off with everything attached.
  4. Before closing up, run the checks in the build guide: every key, the knob, the power key and its light, the screen and a card.

8Fit the rear panel

  1. Mount the USB-C socket in the rear panel and plug its lead into the Pi port marked USB (not PWR IN).
  2. Screw the rear panel on with four M3 × 8 screws.
  3. Check that an RCA plug and a headphone plug both seat fully through their holes.

9Close up

  1. Before closing for good, test card reading with the brass fitted and five cards in the tray.
  2. Lower the lid between the panels and fit its four low-profile screws, by hand.
  3. Stick the feet on, clear of the floor slots and the vents.

Drawings

Generated from case.py, so they match the STLs. Millimetres, measured from the bottom left of each view.

Brass face

Cut it from 0.8 mm brass using Brass-Front-Template.svg. It is drawn at actual size, seen from the front: print it at 100% and check the scale bar measures exactly 100 mm before using it as a pattern. It has the power key's hole, a screen window, a 14.6 mm square hole with rounded corners for each key, the encoder hole and four screw holes, with centre marks for a punch.

The screen window has square corners and the key holes rounded ones, which suits laser or waterjet cutting, or a fretsaw and file. The key caps show any wobble in the key holes, so file them to the line. Deburr, then try it in the printed pocket before sticking it down.

Rebuilding after a change

Edit the values at the top of case.py, then run these from this folder in order. The first rewrites the STLs, the OpenSCAD copy and the brass outline, and reports any part that collides with another. The OpenSCAD file is a generated copy and has not been run through OpenSCAD.

/Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender -b -P build.py
(cd front-board && /Applications/KiCad/KiCad.app/Contents/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/Current/bin/python3 board.py)
/Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender -b -P keycaps.py
/Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender -b -P wood.py (only for the wood-grain version)
python3 drawings.py
/Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender -b -P pictures.py
/Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender -b NFC-Player-Render.blend -P render.py
../.venv/bin/python guide.py

The second line redraws and reroutes the front board, runs KiCad's electrical and design rules checks, and rewrites its Gerber files. Run it whenever you move the keys, the screws or the board's outline. The model checks that parts fit each other and the stand-ins. It cannot check print tolerances, your exact boards, heat, or how well the NFC reader works next to brass and stored cards: those need a bench test.
